item.title: Azure Incident Response: Complete Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Azure cross-tenant synchronization (CTS) can be weaponized for stealthy persistence, letting an attacker inject users from a controlled tenant into a victim tenant with minimal noise.
Key findings:
- The attack requires the Hybrid Administrator role in the victim tenant. Once configured, the attacker adds their tenant as a trusted partner, enabling automatic user provisioning into the victim environment. The critical audit log event to hunt is "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," which captures the attacker's tenant ID and the initiating user's UPN.
- The Audit Log is the only reliable source. Sign-in logs, Provisioning logs, and the Activity log do not record CTS setup. Portal-generated consent pop-ups leave no log trace at all, so GUI-only actions are silent.
- Synchronized users arrive tagged as ExternalAzureAD and B2B, but B2B alone does not confirm CTS abuse. Correlation with the initial "Add a partner" audit event is the only way to distinguish CTS-provisioned accounts from ordinary guest invitations.
- Microsoft records a proxy IP from their own range on the victim side, not the attacker's real source IP. The actual source IP only appears in audit logs on the attacker-controlled tenant, which responders typically cannot access.
Takeaway: Run this KQL against AuditLogs in Microsoft Sentinel: filter OperationName == "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," extract initiating_user, source_ip, and target_tenant.

item.title: Daxin: 13-Year-Old China-Linked Malware Found Still Active on Manufacturer’s Network
item.description:
Chinese-linked Daxin rootkit, first documented in 2022 with roots to 2013, found still running in 2026 on a Taiwanese 🇹🇼 manufacturer's network alongside a previously unknown backdoor called Stupig.
- Daxin is a Windows kernel-mode driver that never makes outbound C2 connections. Instead it monitors incoming TCP traffic for specific patterns and hijacks existing legitimate connections to carry encrypted C2 traffic, making it invisible to tools hunting for suspicious outbound destinations. Multi-hop routing lets operators reach air-gapped hosts through a chain of compromised machines.
- Stupig (kbdus1.dll) persists by registering as a keyboard-layout provider, causing win32k.sys to load it into winlogon.exe at boot. It intercepts usernames prefixed with "stupig" at the login screen and executes the remainder as SYSTEM, before any user authenticates and without generating a logon audit event.
- Both artifacts carry 2013 compile timestamps. Telemetry only appeared May 12, 2026, implying up to 13 years of undetected access. Suspected initial access was a Digiwin SSO portal running end-of-life JDK 1.5/1.6.
Takeaway: Hunt for unsigned or unexpected DLLs loaded into winlogon.exe, and audit keyboard-layout provider registrations in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Keyboard Layouts. Full report from Symantec's Threat Hunter Team contains additional details.

item.title: Invictus Case Study: How We Almost Got Hacked | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
An IR firm turned a failed BEC attempt against itself into a full campaign teardown, tracking the "VendorVandals" from a single phishing email to a multi-country infrastructure network.
- Initial lure arrived as a procurement inquiry from a spoofed US 🇺🇸 pharmaceutical address, referencing a product Invictus IR does not sell. The actor delivered an HTML file via WeTransfer that redirected to an AiTM Microsoft 365 credential-harvesting page at digiusa[.]xyz (104.145.210[.]76), matching EvilProxy framework patterns. WeTransfer delivery is deliberate: it bypasses email security scanners that do not follow outbound links to file-sharing services.
- Infrastructure pivoting via pDNS and hosting fingerprints expanded the picture to six domains and three IPs: propelladata[.]xyz, refactusaonline[.]space, digius[.]space, naronusaonline[.]space, naronusa[.]space, 202.155.8[.]248, and 104.145.210[.]73. Domain registration dates suggest the campaign started around 20 October 2025.
- Targeting spans biotechnology, pharma, lab equipment, industrial distribution, water treatment, and software firms across the US 🇺🇸, Germany 🇩🇪, Spain 🇪🇸, Belgium 🇧🇪, Denmark 🇩🇰, and India 🇮🇳. Lure subjects follow a template: victim name plus "Requirements" or "Technical Specifications and Vendor Registration Form."
Takeaway: Hunt mail logs for HTML file attachments or WeTransfer/Dropbox links in procurement-themed threads.

item.title: Anatomy of a BEC Attack: 2026 Trends | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
A real BEC case dissected end-to-end: AiTM phishing via SharePoint trust chains, PERFECTDATA SOFTWARE abuse, and inbox rules burying fake invoice replies before 1,000 emails flew out.
Key findings:
- Initial access came from a SharePoint file-sharing notification, not a suspicious email. A PDF hosted on a previously compromised tenant linked to an AiTM phishing page harvesting credentials and MFA tokens. Because the sender was a known contact, email security never flagged it. Look for MailItemsAccessed, FileDownloaded, and FileAccessed in the Unified Audit Log, plus Entra sign-ins showing OfficeHome app and user-agent axios/1.11.0 from VPN-associated IPs.
- The threat actor consented to PERFECTDATA SOFTWARE (App ID ff8d92dc-3d82-41d6-bcbd-b9174d163620) days after initial access to silently read and exfiltrate the full mailbox. Block user consent in Entra now; by default any user can grant this.
- Inbox rules (New-InboxRule) routed supplier replies and then all incoming mail to the RSS folder to hide fake invoice responses. Short rule names are a TA tell. Hunt them.
- HardDelete events flagged attacker cleanup attempts. Items purged within 14 days can still be recovered. Those are exactly the emails worth restoring first.
Takeaway: Hunt Entra logs for OfficeHome logins plus axios user-agent, audit consented apps for the PERFECTDATA App ID, and review New-InboxRule events. Full IOC and TTP list is on the Invictus IR GitHub.

item.title: From SQL Injection to Infrastructure-Level RCE: A PostgreSQL Superuser Compromise
item.description:
SQL injection in a government financial portal escalates to unauthenticated RCE via PostgreSQL superuser access, exposing employee PII and full infrastructure control.
- The entry point was pJobNumber in vss00CvStatusData.php, a parameter concatenated directly into a SQL query with no parameterization. A single quote triggered a raw PostgreSQL error, confirming classic error-based SQLi (T1190). UNION SELECT with NULL placeholders revealed a three-column query structure, enabling clean data extraction.
- The web app connected to the database as the native postgres superuser account. That single misconfiguration collapsed every privilege boundary: no escalation needed, the attacker landed with full database control from the first successful injection.
- With superuser access, PostgreSQL system catalogs were wide open. The auditor enumerated public.vss01tpemployee and found employee names, PAN numbers, and financial records. From there, PostgreSQL's COPY TO/FROM and pg_read_file or PROGRAM extensions make OS-level RCE a short step.
- The portal belongs to state financial infrastructure (vsswb). Full unauthenticated RCE on a government network via a single unparameterized parameter is a critical-severity finding, and the disclosed bureaucratic non-response is a reminder that responsible disclosure does not always close the loop.
If you audit web apps backed by PostgreSQL, confirm the DB user in query responses.

item.title: Cloud Ransomware: Trends & Defense Strategies | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Exposed AWS long-term access key led to S3 data exfiltration and ransomware destruction, with versioning disabled before deletion to eliminate recovery options.
- Initial access came from a publicly exposed IAM access key. The key had limited scope, so most recon and persistence attempts (ListServiceQuotas, GetSendQuota, CreateUser calls for accounts named root, adminz, deploy, s3mize, and ses-smtp-user) all returned AccessDenied. The attacker used AWS CLI on a Windows host. The activity began outside CloudTrail's 90-day retention window, so the earliest evidence was gone before the investigation started.
- Exfiltration was confirmed not through CloudTrail (data events were disabled) but through AWS Cost and Usage Reports. GetObject operations generate egress charges recorded in billing data. Sorting the CSV by UsageValue and filtering on DataTransfer-Out or C3DataTransfer-Out Bytes surfaced the transfer volume and time window, even without log visibility.
- Before deleting data, the attacker called GetBucketVersioning to check whether versioning was enabled, then PutBucketVersioning to suspend it. This killed the recovery path before wiping files and dropping a ransom note. The sequence is deliberate and documented in CloudTrail even when data events are off.
Hunt for the GetBucketVersioning then PutBucketVersioning sequence in CloudTrail and alert on it immediately.

item.title: Stop Adversary-in-the-Middle Attacks: Proven Response Tactic | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
AiTM phishing now drives the majority of BEC cases in M365 environments. Microsoft recorded a 146% surge in AiTM detections, roughly 39,000 incidents daily, as MFA adoption pushes attackers toward session token theft.
- Toolkits driving these intrusions include Evilginx, EvilProxy, Modlishka, Mamba 2FA, and Tycoon 2FA. All operate as reverse proxies, sitting between the victim and Microsoft auth to harvest session tokens in real time, bypassing MFA entirely. The stolen token, not the password, is the primary weapon.
- In Entra Sign-In Logs, hunt for OfficeHome as AppDisplayName combined with an empty DeviceId and RiskDetail not equal to "none." The strongest signal is a single SessionId appearing across more than one IP within a 15-minute window, a direct fingerprint of session hijacking (T1539, T1557).
- The Unified Audit Log carries the same pattern using App ID in place of the application name. DeviceProperties absence is meaningful: in the UAL, Device ID only appears if it exists, so its absence is itself an indicator. Cross-reference SessionId anomalies and geographic impossibility across both log sources.
- Remediation requires more than a password reset. Revoke all active sessions via Entra ID, reset MFA registrations, and audit for rogue authenticators added for persistence. Token caching means apps may grant limited attacker access even after revocation, so verify re-authentication is enforced across all clients.

item.title: Introducing KubeForenSys: AKS Forensics Framework | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
KubeForenSys is a new open-source AKS forensics framework from Invictus IR that unifies container logs, RBAC changes, and pod activity into a single KQL timeline, filling critical evidence gaps when Container Insights is not enabled.
Key details:
- The core problem: AKS evidence is decentralized across control plane components, nodes, pods, and containers. Containers are short-lived and Kubelets restart failed ones, destroying logs if not captured in time. Container Insights is opt-in and absent on many clusters.
- KubeForenSys collects eight data types via the Kubernetes API: container logs, cluster events, command history from containers, service accounts, suspicious pods, RBAC bindings, cronjobs, and network policies, then pushes them to a Log Analytics workspace.
- The API-based approach catches what Container Insights misses: exec sessions into containers (bash/cmd into container technique), hostPath mounts indicating volume abuse, and service accounts per namespace, all relevant to the Microsoft Threat Matrix for Kubernetes.
- Output lands in Log Analytics as custom tables (kubelogs_CL and others). A union KQL query stitches them into a single timestamped timeline with a JSON Details column you can filter by container, namespace, or event type.
- The script requires specific Azure RBAC permissions to create resources in the target resource group; review the JSON permission set in the report before deployment.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2078405235433668677

item.title: GraphRunner Guide: Ultimate Defensive Strategies Part II | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
GraphRunner's Microsoft 365 pillage modules leave distinct traces across MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs, Unified Audit Log, and Entra ID Audit Log if you know where to look.
- Invoke-SearchSharePointAndOneDrive and Invoke-SearchMailbox both hit graph.microsoft[.]com/v1.0/search/query first, then follow up with drives or messages endpoints. Hunt with: MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where UserAgent contains "PowerShell" | where RequestUri has_all("graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/drives/","/items/","/content"). Note that SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint requires Microsoft Advanced Auditing and must be manually enabled per mailbox.
- Invoke-SearchMailbox triggers MailItemsAccessed in the UAL, which is your pivot to identify exactly which messages were accessed. Correlate the Graph API call to graph.microsoft[.]com/v1.0/me/messages/ with the InternetMessageID values in MailItemsAccessed to reconstruct what the attacker read and exfiltrated.
- Invoke-ImmersiveFileReader is a blind spot: it generates no MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs entry. Detection relies entirely on the UAL FileDownloaded operation combined with a PowerShell UserAgent. If you are not ingesting UAL into Sentinel, this module is invisible to you.
- Destructive supplemental modules (Invoke-DeleteOAuthApp, Invoke-DeleteGroup, Invoke-RemoveGroupMember) emit DELETE method events in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs and corresponding entries in Entra ID AuditLogs.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2078390058369818933

item.title: GraphRunner Guide: Ultimate Defensive Strategies Part I | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
GraphRunner, a Microsoft Graph post-exploitation toolkit, leaves distinct traces across Entra ID Sign-In logs, Audit Logs, and MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs that defenders can hunt with targeted KQL.
Key findings:
- Authentication via Get-GraphTokens uses device-code flow against Microsoft Graph. Detect it with: SigninLogs | where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" | where ResourceDisplayName == "Microsoft Graph". Token refresh modules (Invoke-RefreshGraphTokens, Invoke-AutoTokenRefresh) produce no reliable log entries, a current blind spot.
- Recon activity surfaces heavily in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs. Invoke-GraphOpenInboxFinder queries graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/[UPN]/mailFolders/Inbox/messages; a PowerShell UserAgent with HTTP 200 responses identifies readable inboxes. Invoke-GraphRecon with PermissionEnum hammers an undocumented estimateAccess beta endpoint, generating a burst of events in seconds.
- Persistence modules write to Azure Audit Logs. Invoke-InjectOAuthApp creates an app registration with broad non-admin-consent permissions (Mail, Files, Teams) and logs three events: "Add application," "Update application," and a secrets management update. The Reply URL field in the "Add application" event holds the attacker-controlled redirect URI.
- Guest invitation and group manipulation via Invoke-InviteGuest and Invoke-AddGroupMember each produce Entra Audit Log entries and MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs hits.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2078359865706090847

item.title: Case Study: The DangerDev@protonmail.me Investigation | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
An exposed AWS IAM access key with AdministratorAccess led to a month-long intrusion: cryptomining, SES-based phishing, fake PayPal domains, and a cross-account backdoor role the defenders almost missed.
- Initial access via a leaked long-term IAM access key (T1552.005). The actor spent two weeks quietly probing SES with GetSendQuota and ListIdentities before escalating, avoiding noisy calls like GetCallerIdentity to stay under detection thresholds.
- Persistence through IAM user DangerDev@protonmail.me, a console login profile, and two cross-account AssumeRole backdoors named AWSLanding-Zones-ConfigRecorderRoles and AWSeservedSSO_* to blend with legitimate role names. External AWS accounts 265857590823 and 671050157472 are confirmed malicious.
- Defense evasion included DeleteUser, DeleteAccessKey, UpdateAccessKey, and notably querying GuardDuty via ListFindings and GetFindings through the RDS console user-agent to monitor their own detection status.
- Impact: GPU instances (p3.16xlarge) for cryptomining, SES abuse for cryptocurrency phishing targeting Japanese 🇯🇵 sites, and four PayPal-loot domains registered via Route 53. LightSail was used as a fallback compute resource when EC2 access was revoked.
Hunt for CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, and CreateRole events in CloudTrail where the principal is not a known automation identity. Flag any AssumeRole from external account IDs not in your allow-list.

item.title: Master eM Client Forensics: A Step-by-Step Analysis | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
eM Client is a legitimate email app repeatedly abused in BEC cases to maintain persistent mailbox access, exfiltrate email, and send phishing at scale from compromised M365 accounts.
Key findings:
- App ID e9a7fea1-1cc0-4cd9-a31b-9137ca5deedd is globally consistent across all tenants. Hunt the Entra ID Audit Log and UAL for three registration events: "Add service principal", "Consent to application", and "Add app role assignment grant to user". The offline_access permission grant is the critical one: it enables refresh tokens that survive password resets.
- Post-registration sign-ins appear in both the Entra sign-in log (with CA policy and risk detail) and the UAL. Filter MailItemsAccessed operations by the eM Client app ID to scope what mail was touched. Note that local email downloads do not generate UAL records, so treat any MailItemsAccessed event tied to this app ID as a presumed exfiltration event.
- Persistence shows up as UpdateInboxRules in the UAL (User-Agent identifies eM Client) and AddFolderPermissions for delegated access grants. Both are detectable and should be cross-referenced with the timeline of the initial app consent.
- Emails sent via eM Client carry a distinctive Message-ID prefix "em" followed by a UUID format, e.g. emd76c6165-abe1-47e3-bef8-a6b6a4a6f467@0a9f8b29[.]com. Run a Message Trace filtered on this pattern to identify outbound phishing sent through the compromised account.

item.title: Proxying to Compromise: SonicWall Secure Mobile Access 0-day Exploitation
item.description:
UTA0533 chained two zero-days against SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, achieving root RCE and deploying memory-injected backdoors. Earliest compromise observed June 22, 2026. Patch now.
- CVE-2026-15409 (SSRF/auth bypass): unauthenticated requests to /wsproxy with User-Agent "SMA Connect Agent" and bmID starting with -3389 tunnel WebSocket connections to localhost-only services including CouchDB (port 1050) and the control service (port 8188). No session cookie required. CVE-2026-15410 (command injection): sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix passes caller-controlled input unsanitized into a path, enabling traversal to /tmp and root-level execution. Affected models: SMA 6210, 7210, 8200v. Patched in 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835.
- UTA0533 dropped ROOTRUN (xzfind, SHA256: 81a9af38...), a setuid ELF binary for privilege escalation, then KNUCKLEBALL (deploy_new.py, SHA256: 8c470301...), a Python loader that injects two JAR agents into the live workplace JVM. Those agents deliver Suo5 (HTTP proxy, agent_wp8.jar) and ORANGETAIL (Behinder-like webshell, agent_wp9.jar) entirely in memory, gated behind a fake User-Agent string.
- Key disk artifacts: /usr/bin/xzfind, /usr/lib/python3.11/site-packages/deploy_new.py, persistence line in /etc/init.d/workplace, and modified /var/lib/unit/conf.json routing /__api__/login and /__api__/logout to 127.0.0.1:8085. On Appliance 2, /var/tmp contained tcpdump captures of cleartext LDAP (port 389) traffic, confirming credential harvesting.

item.title: You Assume Your Logs Are Flowing.
item.description:
Silent log pipeline failures in Microsoft Sentinel create blind spots that look identical to a quiet, healthy SOC, across four distinct failure points that standard health checks miss.
- Agents and connectors can stop sending data with zero alerts. The Heartbeat table query with a reliability filter (active 5 of 7 days minimum) surfaces machines that went silent, while a day-over-day Usage table comparison flags tables that dropped volume by 20-100% or went completely dark. Status labels like "TABLE WENT SILENT" and "CRITICAL DROP" give responders immediate triage priority.
- DCR transformation errors drop rows silently. Enabling error logging per Data Collection Rule exposes these via DCRLogErrors. The Operation table catches workspace-level rejections such as exceeding the 500-column limit on custom tables or V2 custom log schema mismatches. SentinelHealth reveals connector fetch failures (401s, 429s, timeouts) that never reach the DCR layer at all, meaning everything upstream looks healthy while no data is flowing.
- Data can land in the wrong table. Windows Security Events routed to the generic Event table instead of SecurityEvent still get ingested and billed, but detections miss them entirely. A SentinelHealth query comparing DestinationTable to StreamName where they do not match surfaces this misconfiguration.
- Ingestion lag kills near-real-time rules silently.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2078163611370004914

item.title: Inside Qilin Ransomware: Custom Rust Loader and Kernel-Level EDR Killer
item.description:
Qilin ransomware deploys a custom Rust loader with reflective PE loading and a kernel-level EDR killer that surgically unlinks security callbacks and locks product executables before encryption begins.
Key findings:
- The Rust loader performs reflective PE loading within the same process, deobfuscating an embedded payload via per-sample unique DWORD math operations. The MZ header appears after calculation, and Flashpoint built a CPU-emulation unpacker achieving 100% config extraction across samples. Active in the wild since May 2024.
- The EDR killer, sold on illicit markets for $2,000 and packed with the Shanya packer, abuses the legitimate ThrottleStop driver (TechPowerUp) to map physical memory and gain kernel read/write primitives, bypassing driver signing by patching the Code Integrity callback table with a dummy function, then restoring it on exit to dodge PatchGuard.
- Rather than blanket callback removal, Qilin surgically zeroes process, thread, image-load, and registry notify callbacks only for addresses belonging to a hardcoded security product blacklist. It then sets an empty DACL on target executables, making them unlaunchable without deletion, before terminating and permanently preventing restart.
- The malware includes a CIS locale check and skips attacking systems in Russia 🇷🇺 and Belarus 🇧🇾, a standard RaaS geographic exclusion.

item.title: New North Korean campaign uses fake coding interviews to steal developer credentials
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 Contagious Interview campaign (REF9403) hides four-stage OTTERCOOKIE malware inside SVG flag images using steganography, targeting developers via fake coding challenges on community Slack workspaces.
- Infection chain: trojanized Next.js repos (e.g. next-ecommerce-private-main.zip, SHA-256: 3e6360f8) embed Base64 payload fragments inside HTML comments across every SVG flag file in an assets/flags directory. serverValidation.js reads them alphabetically, reassembles the payload, decodes via a custom Check() function, then eval()s the result on every npm run dev or npm start, bypassing Buffer.from and atob detections.
- Four modules deploy in sequence: a browser credential and crypto wallet stealer (masquerades as npm-cache, hits ldb.rightwidth[.]dev/upload and /cldbs, targets 25 extensions including MetaMask and Phantom); a recursive file stealer targeting *.env, *.pem, .ssh, .aws, .bash_history and more (upload.rightwidth[.]dev/upload); a Socket.IO RAT (controller.rightwidth[.]dev) with interactive shell via child_process.exec(); and a clipboard poller every 500ms plus a Windows dropper fetching hostService.exe, printSvc.exe, dhcpSvc.exe disguised as .txt files from file.rightwidth[.]dev.
- Key IOCs: C2 domain rightwidth[.]dev and subdomains; IPs 195.26.248[.]212 and 188.40.64[.]61; seven trojanized repo hashes in the report. All repos had zero AV detections at time of discovery.

item.title: Confused Deputy: Google IdP Universal Account Takeover via Device Code Flow Hijacking
item.description:
Two stacked bugs in Google's OAuth device code flow (RFC 8628) enabled silent, one-click account takeover on any "Sign in with Google" app, including Gmail via IMAP, with no consent screen and no 2FA prompt.
Key findings:
- Bug 1: Google's device-code sign-in session is transferable via URL. The challenge endpoint at accounts.google[.]com/v3/signin/challenge carries an encrypted blob (TL=) anchoring the device poll. Sending that URL to a victim completes the flow under their identity, violating RFC 8628 §5.4 explicitly.
- Bug 2: client_id and scope are never server-side validated against the issued device_code. Swapping YouTube TV's client_id for Google Cloud SDK's, with scope=cloud-platform,compute,appengine.admin, caused the token poll to return elevated cloud tokens, not YouTube tokens.
- Adding prompt=none and a third-party client_id (e.g. Facebook's) reduced victim interaction to opening a link. No consent screen rendered, no 2FA triggered. The connections page logs YouTube TV, not the attacker's client, burying the trace under five clicks and domain knowledge.
- Gmail IMAP access was achievable via XOAUTH2 on imap.gmail[.]com:993 using the substituted token after the Gmail REST API blocked it at the project layer. Full inbox access confirmed.
Reported Feb 25, 2026, fixed Mar 28, 2026, rewarded $13,337. Hunt for anomalous OAuth grants in Google Workspace logs where the connected app shown mismatches the scopes actually granted.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2078088409428435401

item.title: How I Detected an Insider Threat in Splunk When Every Single Action Looked Legitimate
item.description:
Insider threat caught in Splunk: three individually legitimate Windows events correlated into a confirmed PII exfiltration, with no exploit, no failed auth, and no perimeter alert firing.
Key findings:
- The kill chain: Event ID 4663 (file read on C:\CustomerExports\payments_export.csv), Event ID 4104 (PowerShell Compress-Archive via Script Block Logging), and Event ID 5156 (curl.exe outbound on port 4444) each looked clean in isolation. All three on the same host inside 30 minutes equals exfiltration.
- None of these log by default. File System auditing plus a SACL, PowerShell Script Block Logging, and Filtering Platform Connection must be explicitly enabled. If they are off when the attack runs, the evidence was never written.
- Compress-Archive does not spawn a child process, so Event ID 4688 never fired. Process-creation-only detection is blind to PowerShell-native staging. Script Block Logging is not optional for insider threat coverage.
- The Splunk correlation: transaction host maxspan=30m on three OR conditions, then where eventcount >= 3. 27 raw events collapsed into 1 incident spanning 25 minutes on FIN-WKS-04.

item.title: There and Back Again: An Operators Guide on NTLM Relaying Egress
item.description:

item.title: Investigating Persistence Mechanisms in AWS
item.description:
AWS persistence survives containment: IAM backdoors, Lambda code injection, and federated tokens let attackers outlast credential rotations and even account disabling.
- Attackers chain iam:CreateUser with iam:CreateAccessKey and iam:AttachUserPolicy to plant a durable foothold. The trail is in CloudTrail: filter requestParameters.userName for unknown accounts, exclude Get/List/Describe noise, and group by userIdentity.arn plus eventName to surface what permissions were granted and by whom.
- iam:CreateRole or iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy with external account IDs in the Principal block gives attacker-controlled accounts cross-account assume-role access. Hunt CloudTrail for CreateRole and UpdateAssumeRolePolicy events whose policyDocument contains unrecognized account IDs, then pull all sts:AssumeRole calls from those accounts.
- Lambda backdoors (T1059) deploy Python that calls iam:CreateUser, attaches AdministratorAccess, and returns plaintext credentials. Exposure via lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig with authType NONE or apigateway:CreateIntegration makes it internet-reachable. Check older function versions, legitimate-looking code may be a cover layer.
- STS GetFederationToken issues temporary creds that survive the source key's deletion or disabling until they expire naturally. The sessionContext.sessionIssuer field is your pivot: it names the compromised IAM user. Apply a deny-all to that user immediately and hold it until the federated creds expire.

item.title: Forgotten UEFI shims undermining Secure Boot
item.description:
11 forgotten, still-trusted UEFI shims (v0.9 and below) bypass Secure Boot on any system enrolling the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate. CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797 assigned; revoked in Microsoft's June 9 2026 Patch Tuesday dbx update.
- The core risk is not a novel bug: any attacker can copy a vulnerable, Microsoft-signed shim to the EFI System Partition of a target machine regardless of its installed OS, pair it with an old GRUB 2 binary, and execute unsigned code at boot, enabling bootkits like BlackLotus, Bootkitty, or HybridPetya. No memory corruption, no ROP chain required.
- CVE-2026-10797 (shims v0.9 and below): the revocation check and signature verification functions read the signature length from different PE structures. An attacker manipulates the WIN_CERTIFICATE length field so dbx and MokListX comparisons run against garbage, silently bypassing certificate-based revocations for any shim-embedded certificate.
- Pre-v15.3 shims ignore SBAT entirely; pre-v0.9 shims ignore MokListX. An enterprise that revoked a compromised MOK certificate via MokListX is fully exposed if an attacker substitutes one of these old shims, which trusts MokList but skips the denylist.
- 11 PE Authenticode hashes were added to dbx on June 9 2026. Note: the expiration of Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 on June 27 2026 does NOT revoke trust in binaries it signed; certificate expiry has no effect on Secure Boot verification.

item.title: Threat Hunting Case Study: Scattered Spider
item.description:

- Scope matters for triage: a single endpoint hit warrants immediate escalation; the same pattern spread across many machines points to a sanctioned IT deployment.
Hunt for the silent-install command-line pattern in Windows Event logs or your EDR. A clean IOC scan is not a clean bill of health. The HUNTER "AnyDesk Silent Installation" package is free in the Community Edition.

item.title: No single pane of glass: Anatomy of an Azure permission takeover
item.description:

item.title: The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den
item.description:
Python supply chain attacks execute payloads at install time, not runtime. Cisco Talos maps every abuse technique across the package lifecycle, from setup.py hooks to .pth persistence, giving defenders a structured hunt framework.

item.title: WhatsApp forensics in 2026 and what survives end-to-end encryption
item.description:
WhatsApp forensics in 2026: E2E encryption protects the wire, not the device. Spyrtacus and the Cellebrite-Pivovarov case both confirm the endpoint is the target, and the artifacts are richer than most examiners expect.
- Android splits evidence across /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/msgstore.db (live, unencrypted chats), wa.db (contacts), and /sdcard/WhatsApp/Databases/msgstore.db.crypt15 (daily encrypted backup). The 64-byte key at /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key is required to decrypt; crypt15 uses a protobuf-encoded key with rotating parameters that broke older single-format scripts. wa-crypt-tools by ElDavoo handles the full crypt15 pipeline and remains the most maintained open-source option.
- iOS consolidates messages, group metadata, and media references in /private/var/mobile/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/GUID/ChatStorage.sqlite under the ZWAMESSAGE table. Critical detail: ZMESSAGEDATE uses Core Data epoch (seconds since 2001-01-01), not Unix time. Merging Android and iOS timelines without correcting this produces timestamp drift that can look like tampering.
- The Spyrtacus campaign (fake WhatsApp APK delivered via social engineering to ~200 Italian 🇮🇹 users) left no trace in msgstore.db. The evidence lived in SMS history, browser history, package installation timestamps, installer source, and accessibility service grants. A WhatsApp exam that stops at the chat database is an incomplete exam.
